summary.text:
A council that has swapped its PWLB borrowing for short-term local authority money and said so plainly. No new PWLB was taken all year because local authority rates were running about 25 basis points cheaper; long-term PWLB debt fell to £137.6m at an average 3.27%, and the £9.98m that matured had cost 4.09%. The stated plan is to refinance those short-term loans into long-term PWLB when rates fall — paragraph 8.3 puts a date on it, 'around December 2027'.

The pressure is cash. External investments have fallen from £6.2m to £2.68m — a single NatWest call account — and the report is direct about why: overspends, reserves drawn down and a materially higher High Needs DSG deficit. Investment income came in at £966k against a £2.12m budget, and treasury costs finished £654k over. Paragraph 8.5 states there will be a need to replace the internal borrowing with long-term PWLB during the next financial year.

The CFR is £237.3m against £137.6m of PWLB, so about £99.7m sits in internal borrowing and short-term local authority loans combined. The report does not separate the two, so no internal-borrowing figure should be quoted for Calderdale. One officer address is published.

officer.subject: Your December 2027 plan, and the cash that has to last until then
officer.body:
Hi Becky,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Cabinet on 14 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Your annual report does something most don't, which is set out the reasoning behind the borrowing rather than just the balances. Paragraph 8.3 explains exactly why no PWLB was taken all year — short-term local authority money running about 25 basis points cheaper — and then states the plan: refinance into longer-term PWLB when rates fall, with "around December 2027" as the expectation.

That's a clear, dated position, and it's the reason I'm writing rather than anything being wrong with it. The market has moved the other way since. Bank Rate is still 3.75% but the one-year OIS is about 4.11% and the two-year 4.21%, so the curve is pricing a rise rather than a fall. Ten-year certainty money is 5.83% today against 5.72% at the end of March. None of that says December 2027 won't come good — it says the gap between now and then is worth watching weekly rather than at the next report, which is what the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard is for. Ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve.

The part that struck us is the cash side. External investments are down to £2.68m from £6.2m — a single call account — and the report is direct that overspends, reserves and a higher High Needs DSG deficit are behind it. Paragraph 8.5 then says there will be a need to replace the internal borrowing with long-term PWLB during the next financial year. So the refinancing decision may arrive before the rate view does, and that's a harder timing problem than either half on its own.

Two things we can help with. Your PWLB book is priced daily on our side against the DMO's repayment curve, so premiums and discounts are a lookup rather than a piece of work: pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Never as a quote — the DMO's is binding — but the answer changes with the curve and it's worth being able to see it. And the monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows how much appetite there actually is before you commit: July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%, so the market is thinner than the headline suggests.

On training, three fit Calderdale: Interest rate risk, for the short-dated position; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the refinancing when it comes; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data and is the indicator that tells you when internal borrowing stops being the cheaper option — worth a look with CIPFA revising the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for the committee this report goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
